item.title: vCenter CVE-2026-123890: unauth bypass, zero-dayed since September
item.description: Broadcom shipped VMSA-2026-0009 Thursday, and CVE-2026-123890 inside it is the one to drop everything for: an unauthenticated authentication bypass in the VMware Directory Service, CVSS 9.8, no workaround. The same day, Mandiant and Google Threat Intelligence published the rest of the story: a suspected China-nexus spy crew they track as Armory Castle used it as a zero-day against live vCenter servers starting in early September. More than two months of runway against your hypervisor management plane. CISA has not added it to KEV as of the November 18 catalog, but CISA has put ten earlier vCenter flaws on that list, and a bug a state crew has been driving through vmdird since early September carries better exploitation evidence than any published PoC.

item.title: Java4Shell CVE-2026-114938: pre-auth RCE in Java's Base64 decoder
item.description: Oracle shipped its November 2026 Critical Security Patch Update on November 17, and one bug inside deserves its own emergency: CVE-2026-114938, nicknamed Java4Shell, an out-of-bounds heap write in the HotSpot Base64 decoder. Security firm Calif released the full write-up and PoC ahead of the coordinated disclosure, and CISA put out a same-day alert urging immediate patching. No exploitation in the wild has been confirmed and the bug is not on CISA’s KEV catalog as of the November 17 feed. CISA didn’t wait for the catalog, and neither should you: I’d patch every Java 17+ runtime this week.

item.title: The Whistle: 61,000 probe pull requests, a stolen cookie into XCP-ng, and Nvidia's interim era
item.description: Stolen GitHub credentials sat at the front of this week’s news: a campaign that probed its way into 61,764 repositories in under two days and exfiltrated credentials from at least 1,835 of them. Behind it ran a takeover chain in Xen Orchestra that ended at XCP-ng root, and an AI-vendor breach whose third chapter reached into Notion’s customer set. On the product side, AWS shipped an emulator built end to end by agents, Google cut the nodepool ceremony out of TPU scheduling, Rust passed 1.100 with a type that took a decade, and Nvidia moved into an interim era without its founder. Security leads, then everything else.

item.title: Critical Apache HTTP/2 RCE: CVE-2026-119618 fixed in 2.4.71
item.description: Apache shipped 2.4.71 on Wednesday with a fix for CVE-2026-119618, a race condition in mod_http2 that lets an unauthenticated client corrupt heap memory and execute code with the web server’s privileges. Releases 2.4.55 through 2.4.70 are in scope whenever HTTP/2 is enabled. There are no confirmed in-the-wild exploits and no CISA KEV entry yet. I’d patch this week anyway.

item.title: MongoDB CVE-2026-118383: pre-auth UAF, patch replica sets
item.description: MongoDB shipped fixed releases on Tuesday for CVE-2026-118383, a use-after-free that can kill a replica set’s freshly elected primary before it accepts a write. The scores are already in: NVD rates 10.0 on CVSS 3.1, and MongoDB’s CNA puts it 9.5 on v4.0. There’s no CISA KEV entry and MongoDB says it’s unaware of exploitation attempts, but a proof of concept is public on GitHub. Patch every replica set member this week.

item.title: The Whistle: Chrome's eighth zero-day, Qubole's trusted path, and an AI proof of Signal
item.description: Google patched Chrome’s eighth in-the-wild zero-day of the year, Wiz published an October attack that walked through the front door Qubole customers built for their own data platform, and a researcher’s 33 zero-days made an RMM vendor unplug its own hosted service. Anthropic put a security model behind a verification program and a footnote, Google’s Carbon-powered agents produced a formal proof of Signal’s protocol implementation, and AWS gave every EKS pod the option of its own hardware-isolated virtual machine at no extra charge. France named Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Corps as the source of the freezer attacks, and the queue behind those stories ran from Barracuda email appliances to SonicWall MFA skips. Security leads, then everything else.

item.title: The Whistle: 948 Linux root paths closed by a model, the cold chain hacked, and gVisor joins the CNCF
item.description: OpenAI shipped its cybersecurity model and the workload that proves it in the same week: GPT-6 Cyber powered the pipeline that validated and patched 948 Linux privilege-escalation flaws for about $1.2 million in API credits. On the other side of the ledger, Chainalysis disclosed that password hashes and live session tokens for all of its users were exposed to an attacker whose only public description is a phrase the company never defined. Anthropic explained why it will not fix the cross-machine Claude Dispatch hole it has known about since May, Sekoia mapped an SVR watering-hole campaign that hunts phones through already-patched devices, and the European cold-chain attacks reached France’s blood service. Zyxel’s June firmware fixed the sibling of the bug its attackers actually used, Japan announced a funded national cyber package, and Anthropic’s amended IPO filing turned “recursive self-improvement” into official risk language while Tencent’s launch post sold the same idea as a roadmap. On the cloud side, Google donated its agent runtime stack to the CNCF ahead of KubeCon, and AWS turned Hive-to-Iceberg migration into a managed job. Security leads, then everything else.

item.title: The Whistle: Special Bulletin - OpenSSH password bypass (CVE-2026-123158) on musl systems
item.description: OpenSSH shipped an emergency release one day after learning of the bug, with Damien Miller telling musl-libc operators to disable password auth IMMEDIATELY. CVE-2026-123158 at CVSS 8.1 lets an attacker log into any passwordless account with a single sent password, first connection, every time. glibc distributions and PAM-using systems are not affected, which is why your Ubuntu fleet is safe. Your Alpine containers with an sshd inside are another matter.

item.title: The Whistle: a Brotli patch wave, a 16-year-old UEFI hole, and Anthropic files to go public
item.description: One bug in a shared library owned the week. A buffer overflow in Google’s Brotli decoder was fixed in the library’s source in February, never released as an update, and spent the rest of the year bundled inside every runtime that links it. This October the catch-up finally ran: coordinated patches across Node.js, Python, Go and the proxy tier, and Microsoft shipped out-of-band .NET fixes on October 25. A 16-year-old UEFI vulnerability surfaced the other way, through a broken embargo. A campaign running on stolen GitHub tokens planted more than 13,500 secret-dumping workflows. Binance lost $6.3 billion to a compromised laptop in 20 minutes. Both sides of the exploit pipeline ran on models this week: Anthropic published a kernel root exploit written by Claude, Epoch AI pushed a Z.ai open-weight model through published-but-unshipped Firefox fixes at about $1,000 a target, AWS made machine-speed vulnerability remediation generally available, and Google gated its new cybersecurity model to defenders first. Security leads, then the rest.

item.title: The Whistle: Special Bulletin - GitLab's CI/CD regex RCE (CVE-2026-97229) joins CISA's KEV catalog
item.description: Two Mondays ago this bug led our patch notes. This week CISA put it in the KEV catalog, Alpine disclosed how close the attackers got, and the fix turned out to be a Ruby build change a GitLab version string cannot prove.

item.title: The Whistle: LiteLLM's poisoned release train, hacker panels left open, and OpenAI lands on Google Cloud
item.description: The release pipeline of LiteLLM, the model-gateway library, was emptied with three engineers’ stolen GitHub tokens. The operators of an open-source AI pentest platform left their control panels answering on the open internet, complete with target lists and API keys. The platforms that hold agent secrets for a living spent the week telling everyone to rotate everything. The CVE drumbeat stayed loud enough that this blog ran four special bulletins between Tuesday and Friday (PHP2Shell, the eMudhra CA compromise, the ATS and Traefik flaws, the Azure configuration service 10.0, VeloCloud and Collabora), so the vulnerability list lives there; this weekly holds the stories. Security leads below, then the cloud and model news: an ingress gateway for ECS, a security read on last week’s Lambda Web Functions launch, native PyTorch backends for both Trainium and TPU, rivals’ models landing on Google Cloud, Python 3.15, TypeScript in Rust, and three new model entries closing the week.

item.title: The Whistle: Special Bulletin - VeloCloud, Collabora CODE, Prime Mover, and Python's CA Denylist
item.description: Between digests: two KEV additions sit on management planes under active attack, a WordPress plugin whose fix beat its advisory, and a 9.4 on CPython’s ssl.

item.title: The Whistle: Special Bulletin - mTLS bypasses in Traffic Server and Traefik
item.description: A short alert between digests: Traffic Server’s Tuesday release fixes fifteen flaws and two of them hand out the wrong client certificate identity; Traefik patched a second connection-identity bug in the same month on related plumbing; and Red Hat is pulling two roots out of its system CA bundle over the eMudhra key leak. mTLS origins, meet your change window.

item.title: The Whistle: Special Bulletin - php2shell and the eMudhra CA keys
item.description: Not the Monday digest: PHP shipped an emergency release this morning for two leaked-then-patched core RCEs, eight eMudhra intermediate CA keys are compromised, and Cisco and Oracle both emptied their patch trucks.

item.title: The Whistle: Root Through a Mail Gateway, an Intrusion Run on 51 Agents, and Deno's Clock Starts
item.description: The appliance beat returned to the top this week: a mail gateway and a VPN, both rooted through unauthenticated bugs that were in use before they had fixes. Below them sits the more interesting story: an initial access broker ran a campaign on Claude Code, a cluster of 51 specialized agents, and an open-source pentest framework, then leaked its own working directory, so the intruder’s playbook is readable in its own session logs. Appliances first, Meta’s GitHub and the agent stories after, cloud and model news closer to the end.

item.title: The Whistle: An npm Worm With a Hostage Token, a Sandbox for Agent Governance, and 372 Proofs Nobody Has Read Yet
item.description: Security owned the week again, and not subtly. An npm release shipped with a dead-man’s switch wired to a stolen credential. Registries for Ghana, Sierra Leone, and American Samoa got bent into a certificate-forgery kit for Google domains. The Wikimedia Foundation published its own account of “rogue” OpenAI agents touching its platforms. Against that, the constructive item of the week: AWS shipped Strands Box, an agent sandbox built on the idea that someone outside the agent’s process should judge what it did, not just what it asks for. Security first, then that, then the rest of the week.

item.title: The Whistle: FortiMail Burns, an Agent Ransacks a Security Nonprofit, and the AI Security Race Splits in Two
item.description: Most weeks the hardest call is which lane leads. Not this one: the perimeter devices went first, then the AI agent stack, and both stories are still getting worse. Cloud news was comparatively quiet, which somehow feels appropriate.

item.title: The Whistle: MTurk Shuts Off, OpenAI Goes Agentic, and the Cloud Giants Learn to Share (a Little)
item.description: Welcome to a new recurring feature. Each week I’ll round up the announcements that actually mattered across AWS, Google Cloud, open source, and frontier AI – with opinions attached, because news is cheap and judgment isn’t.
